Lower to minimum. Pour the beaten eggs in the thinnest possible stream while stirring slowly in one direction. Stop stirring and let them set for 10 seconds.|Take out Chloé's bowl now
Off the heat: vinegar, white pepper, sesame oil. Taste and adjust, this is where the dish is tuned.
Spring onion and coriander in each bowl as you serve.
no: The heat comes from white pepper.
Not from chilli. The 辣 in 酸辣湯 is a generous dose of white pepper, a teaspoon and a half for 1.2 litres at minimum. And it goes in off the heat, because cooking dulls its bite.
Vinegar last, off the heat.
It evaporates. Poured in during the simmer, the soup loses its acidity and you end up with a flat broth you can no longer rescue.
Cornstarch before the egg.
A thickened broth holds the ribbons in suspension. In a thin broth the egg sinks and clumps at the bottom.
The egg ribbons.
Heat at minimum, the thinnest possible stream, and stir slowly in one direction. Vigorous stirring shatters the ribbons into specks.
For Chloé
Take out her bowl at the end of step 8, before the pepper and vinegar. Then add half a teaspoon of vinegar and a pinch of pepper to her bowl. She gets the same soup, dosed for her.
suanla.p: Served alongside the dishes and the rice, not as a starter. With one stir-fried meat dish it makes a complete meal and replaces the vegetable.

tofubraise.n: Braised tofu with shiitake and pak choi
g: Firm tofu, pack marked 煎炸

g.t: The red pack at Pak Took, the one whose photo shows golden cubes. The green 蒸煮拌 is soft and would fall apart. Firmer still: 板豆腐 from the tofu stall at the wet market.

s: Press the tofu before anything else: set the block between two sheets of kitchen paper, a plate on top, a tin on the plate. 15 to 20 minutes. Blotting alone is not enough.
Cut into even 2 cm cubes.
Oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Sear the tofu in two batches, a single layer, with space between the pieces.|500 g at once steam each other
4 minutes per side untouched. As long as a piece sticks, the crust has not formed. Once it has, it releases by itself. Set aside on a plate.
If water appears in the bottom of the pan, raise the heat and let it evaporate before going on. Tofu does not brown in water, it steams.
Wipe the pan, fresh oil. Stir-fry the shiitake 4 minutes. Wait until the pan goes dry again and they start to colour, that is where their flavour concentrates.
Garlic and ginger, 30 seconds.
Stir the bowl of sauce and pour it in. Return the tofu with a spatula, leaving behind the liquid it released while waiting on the plate.|That liquid would dilute the sauce just before it thickens
Simmer 5 minutes covered. Push the pan back and forth rather than stirring, browned tofu is fragile.
Lay the pak choi on top, cover another 3 minutes, it steams in the sauce. Off the heat, sesame oil and spring onion.
no: Which tofu to buy.
It has to be firm. At Pak Took that is the red-labelled pack marked 煎炸, the one whose photo shows golden cubes. The green one marked 蒸煮拌 is soft and will disintegrate in the pan.
Press, then two batches.

The two mistakes that cost you the golden crust. Unpressed tofu releases its water into the pan. An overloaded pan produces the same result, the pieces steam each other. Either way the tofu stays white and eventually falls apart.
Do not try to brown every side.
With supermarket tofu, turning each cube a second time breaks more pieces than it adds colour. Two well-coloured sides are plenty.
Pak choi at the end, on top.
It steams in the sauce in three minutes and keeps its colour. Stirred in earlier it turns khaki and releases water.
For Chloé
A mild dish with nothing to remove. Golden tofu is far more approachable for children than plain tofu.
tofubraise.p: Complete with the rice. If you want to serve something alongside, a clear soup rather than a second stir-fry.

boulettes.n: Lion's head meatballs with Chinese cabbage
g: Fresh water chestnuts, in 3 mm dice
s: Soak the shiitake 30 minutes in warm water. Keep the soaking water, strained, it goes into the braise.
Chop the water chestnuts with a knife into 3 mm dice. Do not blitz them.|Their crunch is what lightens the meatball; pulverised, they serve no purpose at all

In a large bowl, the pork with the ginger, spring onion, egg, cornstarch, Shaoxing, soy sauce, sugar, salt and white pepper. Stir with chopsticks in one direction only, 2 minutes.|Changing direction breaks the fibres that are busy aligning, and it is those fibres that hold the meatball together

Pour in the iced water in three goes, still turning the same way, waiting for full absorption before adding more.|This water is what makes the meatballs tender; without it they are as dense as a burger patty

Work in the water chestnuts. Then take the whole mass in your hand and throw it hard back into the bowl, about fifteen times.|The step nobody does and the one that decides everything: unslapped filling falls apart during the braise
Shape 6 meatballs the size of a tennis ball, smooth them between two wet palms, chill 20 minutes.
Line the bottom of the casserole with the white ribs of the cabbage, then the leaves on top.|The meatballs must never touch the metal: they catch and break when you try to lift them

Oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Brown the meatballs 2 minutes per side without moving them, three at a time.|Until the crust has formed they are fragile; turning them too soon splits them in two
Set them gently on the cabbage. Add the shiitake, the stock, the strained soaking water and the dark soy sauce. The liquid should reach two thirds up the meatballs, not cover them.
Cover and simmer 50 minutes at the smallest possible bubble. Never stir.|A proper boil breaks them up within half an hour
Serve with the rice, spooning broth and cabbage over each bowl.
no: Medium-fat, definitely not lean.
You need at least 30% fat. At the wet market, ask for 三七肥瘦, seven parts lean to three parts fat. Lean pork gives a dry, rubbery meatball, and no technique makes up for it.
Stir one way, then slap.
Both gestures do the same thing, aligning the proteins into a network. That network is what holds the meatball together through fifty minutes of braising.
The cabbage is not a garnish.
It is a mattress, it flavours the broth and it absorbs the rendered fat. By the end it is meltingly soft and it is often what children prefer.
For Chloé
Nothing spicy, nothing to remove. The meatball is soft and cuts with a spoon, and the braised cabbage is sweet. Give her half a meatball with plenty of cabbage and rice.
boulettes.p: Rice and nothing else, the cabbage is the vegetable. Double the quantities without hesitation: reheated the next day in a clear broth with noodles and a green, the leftover meatballs make a complete dinner in fifteen minutes.

g.t: The cut to ask for at the wet market. Fat and sinew included, they are what melt into gelatine and make the sauce. A lean grilling cut will give dry, stringy meat.
Roll-cut, in irregular 4 cm pieces: the edges catch the sauce.
Three go into the blanching water, three into the braise.
Two whole for the blanching, the third chopped for the finish.
Thicker and darker than Ceylon cinnamon, in the loose spice section.
Optional. Left whole they perfume without real heat, and lift out before serving.
Two tablespoons for the blanching water, two for the braise.
For the mahogany colour, not for salt.
The large amber crystals. Failing that, 2 tsp of caster sugar.

s: Put the beef in a pan, cover with cold water, add 3 slices of ginger, 2 whole spring onions and 2 tbsp Shaoxing. Bring to the boil.|Starting cold draws out the blood and impurities; dropped into boiling water the meat seals and keeps them inside
Skim the grey foam for 3 to 4 minutes, until no more rises. Drain and rinse in hot water. Dry the cubes well on kitchen paper.

Oil and rock sugar in a casserole over medium-low heat. Let it melt without stirring until it reaches the colour of maple syrup, about 3 minutes.|One second too long and the caramel turns dark brown: it becomes bitter and you have to start again. If you would rather not risk it, skip this step and add an extra ½ tbsp of dark soy sauce
Tip the beef into the caramel and turn it for 2 minutes to coat. It should gleam.
Add the remaining ginger, the garlic, star anise, cassia, bay and chillies. 30 seconds.
Pour the remaining Shaoxing around the hot sides, then both soy sauces. Cover with boiling water to 2 cm above the meat.|Cold water on hot meat contracts it and it will stay tough to the end
Cover and simmer 1 h to 1 h 15, at the smallest possible bubble, one breaking now and then.|A hard boil breaks down the outside of the cubes long before the centre gives
Test: a chopstick should pass through a cube with slight resistance. If it still resists, continue in 15-minute stretches.
Rinse the cut potatoes under cold water to remove surface starch, dry them, then add with the carrot. Taste the broth and salt now.
Continue uncovered for 25 to 30 minutes.|Added at the start, the potatoes disintegrate completely and their starch thickens the sauce far too early, so it catches on the bottom
Never stir with a spoon: take the casserole by the handles and shake it back and forth. The potatoes are fragile and a stirred sauce turns cloudy.
The sauce thickens on its own from the potato starch, no cornstarch is needed. Too thin, continue 5 minutes uncovered. Too thick or catching, a ladle of boiling water.
Remove the star anise, cassia, bay and chillies. Scatter with chopped spring onion.
no: The cut makes the dish.

You need 牛腩, brisket, with its fat and sinew. It is the collagen melting into gelatine that gives the sauce its glossy body. A lean cut sold for the pan has nothing to melt: after two hours it will be dry and stringy.
Blanch, and start from cold.
The step everybody skips, and the one that decides how clear the broth is. Start cold so the impurities rise, skim until the grey foam stops.
Potatoes last, 25 minutes.
The one real way to ruin this dish. Added at the start they end up as purée and their starch thickens the braise for an hour, the bottom of the pot catches and takes on a burnt taste.
Shake, do not stir.
Once the potatoes are in, a spoon breaks the pieces and clouds the sauce. You lift the casserole and shake it.
For Chloé

The dish is naturally mild, the star anise and cassia are aromatic but not hot. Leave the chillies whole and lift them out before serving, or leave them out entirely. The soft potatoes and the meat that shreds apart are easy to eat with a spoon.
boeufpdt.p: Rice and a bright green vegetable to cut through the braise: garlic cauliflower or stir-fried kale. The leftovers are better the next day, once the sauce has finished penetrating the meat.

g.t: The loose, long-stemmed variety stir-fries far better than the tight European cauliflower.

s: Break the cauliflower into bite-sized florets. Dry them well.
Wok over high heat with the oil. Add the cauliflower and leave it untouched for 2 minutes so it colours.
Toss for another 2 minutes. Brown patches should appear.
Pour the water around the rim of the wok, cover immediately, 3 minutes. The steam cooks the centre.
Uncover, add the chopped garlic, 30 seconds.
Oyster sauce, soy sauce, sugar, salt and white pepper. Toss 1 minute uncovered until the liquid has gone.
no: Colour it before you cook it.
White, boiled cauliflower has no flavour at all. The first two minutes untouched over high heat create the brown patches that make the whole dish.

g.t: Firm and low-starch. Floury mashing potatoes will collapse into mush in the wok.
Optional but classic. It brings colour and a different kind of crunch.

g: Dried red chillies, deseeded and cut into lengths

g.t: Cut into lengths rather than halved: three times the surface in contact with the oil, so far more heat. Seeds removed, you get the fragrance without the dry burn.
Optional. They numb slightly and mark it out as the Sichuan version.
White, not Chinkiang: black vinegar is too sweet and too dark for this dish. Half of it evaporates against the wok, hence the slightly generous dose.
What was missing. Salt and vinegar alone give a clean but hollow dish: the soy brings the savoury base the acidity leans on.
Less than before, because the soy sauce already brings salt. Taste before adding more.

s: Peel the potatoes, slice them 2 mm thick, then cut each slice into 2 mm matchsticks. A julienne grater does the job in thirty seconds.|Uneven sticks cook unevenly: the thinnest are soft while the thickest are still raw
Drop them into a large bowl of cold water as you go.

Stir with your hand, the water turns white. Tip it away, refill, and repeat three times until it stays clear.|The step that decides everything. Surface starch is what welds the sticks together and turns the dish into a pasty mass. Rinsed, they stay separate and crunchy
Leave them in cold water until the last moment, then drain and dry them in a tea towel.|Wet, they spit in the oil and steam instead of frying
Line everything up beside the wok. The cooking takes three minutes and there will be no time to cut anything.

Wok over high heat with the oil, hot but not smoking. Chillies and Sichuan peppercorns, 15 seconds, until the chillies darken.|In smoking oil they blacken within five seconds and the bitterness takes over the whole dish
Garlic, 10 seconds. Raise to maximum heat.
Tip in all the matchsticks at once, with the green pepper. Toss constantly for 2 minutes.
Salt, sugar, soy sauce, and half the vinegar poured onto the hot side of the wok. Another 30 seconds.|On the side it vaporises and perfumes everything; poured into the middle it wets and softens
Taste a stick: it should snap clearly under the tooth, with only the core giving way.|One minute too long and it turns soft and floury, with no way back
Off the heat, the rest of the vinegar, the spring onion and a drizzle of sesame oil.
no: Rinse the starch, three times.

That is the whole recipe. Without rinsing the sticks weld into a grey, sticky mass; with rinsing they stay individual and snappy. Three changes of water, until it stays clear, and keep them in cold water until the moment you cook.
It is a crunchy dish.

The surprise for a French palate: the potato is not meant to be meltingly soft here, it should snap like a barely seared raw vegetable. The vinegar plays its part, keeping the pectin firm and stopping the sticks collapsing.
Pale, but not quite.

The orthodox version stays almost translucent, with only the red dots of the chillies, which is why Chinkiang vinegar is ruled out. The spoonful of soy sauce added here pulls the colour towards light amber. It is a deliberate trade: the dish gains the savoury base it lacked and loses a little of its paleness. If you would rather have it the other way round, swap the soy for 1 tsp of chicken bouillon powder, 雞粉, which does not colour.
A julienne grater.
A few dollars in any neighbourhood hardware shop, and you go from ten minutes of knife work to thirty seconds, with perfectly even sticks.
For Chloé
Without chilli or Sichuan pepper it is a mild, tangy, crunchy dish that children eat very happily. Fry the chillies whole and lift them out before serving if you want some heat for yourself.
tudousi.p: A 下飯菜, a dish that accompanies rice. It goes with any meat dish in this book and is made last, while everything else waits.

g.t: The cut makes the dish. Ask for fresh 梅頭 at the wet market, never frozen: the fat runs evenly through it and the meat stays tender. Tenderloin is too lean and comes out dry and stringy.
For the dry coating. A thin dry crust holds far better than a thick batter, which peels off in sheets the moment it meets the sauce.
Fresh, not tinned. Tinned pineapple is already cooked, soft, and drowns the dish in its syrup. A whole pineapple costs a few dollars at the market.

g: Red and green peppers, in squares

g.t: Use 子薑, young ginger, if you can find it: more tender and less sharp, and it is what the restaurants use.
Yes, ketchup, and it is exactly what the kitchens here use: it brings the gentle acidity, the sugar and the colour all at once.
Optional, and the detail of the old houses. Hawthorn rounds the sweet and sour out instead of letting it clash. Sold in packets in any neighbourhood herbal shop.
Slaked in 1 tbsp of cold water, and kept back for the very end.
For deep frying. Strained once cool, it will serve two or three more times.

s: Cut the pork collar into even 2.5 cm cubes.|Smaller and they dry out before they colour; larger and the coating burns while the centre is still raw
Mix the meat with the soy sauce, salt, sugar and white pepper. Leave for 20 minutes.|The Hong Kong chef adds almost nothing here: just enough to season, so the flavour of the 梅頭 stays in front

Meanwhile mix the ketchup, tomato paste, vinegar, sugar, water, salt and hawthorn in a bowl. Taste, and correct it now.|This is the last moment the sauce can be corrected. Once it is in the wok everything moves too fast, and a sauce that is too sharp or too sweet cannot be saved
Cut the pineapple and peppers, chop the garlic, slice the ginger. Line everything up beside the wok along with the slaked cornstarch.
Crack the egg over the meat and mix by hand until every cube is coated.

Mix the cornstarch and flour in a shallow dish. Roll the cubes through it one by one, then shake off the excess.|A thin dry veil, not a thick layer. Shaking is not optional: loose flour falls into the oil and burns in it

Heat the oil to 160°C. Fry the cubes in two batches, 3 to 4 minutes, until cooked through but still pale. Drain.|Gentle oil first: the meat cooks through without drying out. Straight into 190°C and the crust would be golden with the inside raw

Raise the oil to 190°C. Return the cubes for 1 minute, until properly golden. Drain on a rack, not on paper.|The second fry drives out the oil the first one drew in: that is what makes the crust dry and crisp. On paper the steam stays underneath and softens the bottom of each piece

Tip out the oil, keeping one spoonful. Garlic and ginger 15 seconds, peppers 1 minute, pineapple 30 seconds. Set aside.|The peppers should stay crunchy and the pineapple just warmed through, not collapsed

Pour the sauce into the wok, bring to a simmer, then trickle in the slaked cornstarch. Stir until it coats the back of a spoon.|Too thin and it slides off and sogs; too thick and it clumps. It should gleam and hold
Return the vegetables, then the pork. Toss for 15 seconds, no more, and tip it onto the dish.|The countdown starts here. Every extra second in the sauce is crispness lost
Spring onion over the top, and straight to the table.
no: Crispness lasts two minutes.

That is the whole difficulty of the dish, and the reason delivered sweet and sour pork is always soft. The sauce must be ready, thickened and glossy before the pork joins it, and the dish goes straight to the table. If you have to wait for someone, serve the sauce separately and combine at the last moment.
Two fries, two temperatures.

160°C first to cook, 190°C after to dry and colour. The second fry is not cooking anything, it is expelling the oil the first one drew in. Skip it and you get a pale, greasy crust that collapses the moment it meets the sauce.
The cut: 梅頭.

Also written 脢頭 by some butchers, it is the collar, the piece above the shoulder. Fat and lean alternate through it, which is what stands up to frying. Tenderloin has nothing to defend itself with and comes out dry. Ask for it fresh rather than chilled.
No onion, and not as a compromise.

The most common restaurant version uses it, but a Hong Kong chef's recipe published in Apple Daily uses only pineapple, peppers, garlic and spring onion. The sweetness of the pineapple and the crunch of the peppers do the work.
咕嚕肉 or 咕咾肉.
Both spellings mean the same dish: 咕嚕肉 in Hong Kong, 咕咾肉 in Taiwan and in older texts. The original name was 古老肉, the old dish, and all three sound almost the same.
For Chloé

This is the Chinese dish children ask for: sweet, golden, no chilli. For her, lift out her share of the fried pork before the final toss and give her a little sauce on the side, so her crust stays intact.
gulao.p: A Sunday lunch dish: the frying needs room and attention, and it has to be eaten scalding, within the minute. With white rice and a stir-fried green vegetable it is a full meal for three.

g.t: Ask for 牛柳 at the wet market, it is exactly the cut this dish uses. Put it in the freezer for 20 minutes before slicing and the slices will be far more even.
The secret behind restaurant-tender beef. No more than that, or it tastes soapy.

g: Red and green peppers, in strips

g.t: Black and syrupy. It is there for colour, not salt.
Whole, without exception. Ready-ground is flat.

s: Slice the beef 5 mm thick, against the grain.|With the grain, every slice keeps its long fibres and stays chewy whatever the marinade does
Mix the beef with the marinade, working it for a minute until the meat turns tacky. Leave 20 minutes.
Crush the peppercorns in a mortar into coarse shards. Divide into two halves.
Mix the sauce in a bowl.

Smoking oil in the wok. Sear the beef in two batches, 1 minute per side untouched. Still pink in the middle. Set aside.|Two batches, not one: 500 g at once drops the wok temperature and the meat releases its water instead of searing
Remaining oil, the first half of the pepper, 20 seconds. Garlic and ginger, 20 seconds.
Celery 1 minute, then peppers 2 minutes. They stay crunchy.
Stir the bowl of sauce then pour it in. Let it thicken for 1 minute at a hard boil.|Serve Chloé's portion now
Return the beef, 30 seconds. Off the heat, the butter and the second half of the pepper.
no: Why 牛柳.

牛柳 means beef fillet cut into strips, and it is the name the cut carries at the wet market. The dish is a Cantonese restaurant classic, where it often arrives on a sizzling plate. At home, a properly hot wok and butter at the end give the same result.
Pepper in two stages.
The first half cooks in the oil and gives depth, the second goes in off the heat and gives aroma. Putting it all in at the start leaves only bitterness.
No onion.
Onion is normally the star alongside the peppers. Celery brings the same crunch plus a vegetal bitterness that stands up to the pepper.
For Chloé
Serve her portion after step 7, before the last half of the pepper.
bpbeef.p: Served with the hand-torn cabbage with pork: the cabbage first, the beef last.

g: Flank or skirt steak, in strips

g.t: Flank and skirt are hard to find under those names here. Ask for 牛柳 at the wet market and slice it yourself, against the grain.
The original uses half an orange; a reader found the orange flavour too faint and the author agreed it should go up. Use a whole one.

g: Fresh red and green chillies, chopped

g.t: Three deseeded for a mild version, up to six with their seeds for the full one.

s: Peel the zest with a vegetable peeler, taking only the orange-coloured layer, then cut it into fine julienne.|The white pith underneath is frankly bitter. If your strip of zest has a white lining, scrape it flat with a knife

Juice the orange. The juice splits into two equal halves, one for the marinade, one for the sauce.|The acidity of the juice in the marinade tenderises the meat; the juice in the sauce gives shine and flavour
Slice the beef into strips, against the grain.

Mix the meat with the marinade ingredients and work it until all the liquid has been absorbed. Leave 10 minutes.|If liquid is still sitting in the bottom of the bowl, keep massaging: only once absorbed has it done its job
Mix all the sauce ingredients in a bowl and set aside.
Line everything else up beside the wok. The cooking takes three minutes in total.

Wok on maximum heat with 2 tbsp oil. Sear the beef just until the surface turns pale, then take it out.|Still pink at the core. It goes back into the wok later, and the second cooking is what finishes it
Discard the liquid that has collected in the bottom of the wok.|The meat always releases a little. Left there, it stops the aromatics frying and dilutes the sauce
Add the last 1 tbsp of oil. Zest, chillies, ginger and garlic, until fragrant, about thirty seconds.
Return the beef and toss for 1 minute.
Stir the bowl of sauce, since the cornstarch settles to the bottom, then pour it in all at once.

Kill the heat as soon as the sauce has thickened and the meat is evenly coated. Serve immediately.|Thirty seconds too long and flank steak, which is very lean, turns tough. That is the classic failure of this dish
no: Where this recipe comes from.

It is Red House Spice's 橙味牛肉, taken from 2 to 3 servings. The rest is faithful with one exception: the author uses the zest of half an orange and I use a whole one, because one of her readers found the orange too faint and she agreed.
The orange is used twice, differently.

Half the juice goes into the marinade, where its acidity tenderises the meat, and the other half into the sauce, where it gives shine and aroma. The zest only arrives in the wok: it is what really carries the orange flavour, the juice alone is too faint.
The white pith.
You take only the orange-coloured skin. The white layer underneath is bitter and that bitterness does not cook away. A sharp vegetable peeler, then scrape the back of the strip if you need to.
Two very short cookings.

Flank steak is lean and has no collagen: it has no margin at all. You sear it just until it pales, take it out, and it only returns for a final minute. The signal to stop is the sauce thickening, not a timer.
For Chloé

The chilli is what makes the dish, but it is entirely in the aromatics, so it cannot be removed afterwards. For a version she will eat, three deseeded chillies are enough: the fragrance stays without the burn. Put chopped fresh chilli on the table for yourself.
orangebeef.p: Plain rice and nothing else: the sauce is short and highly perfumed, and a second spicy dish would bury it. A blanched green on the side if you want a vegetable.

g.t: A loose head with pale, supple leaves. Not the hard green cabbage.

g: Fresh pork belly, in 3 cm slices

g.t: With well-alternated layers of fat and lean.

s: Tear the cabbage by hand into palm-sized pieces. Never with a knife.
Wash and dry it really thoroughly, in a salad spinner if you have one.
Wok over medium heat, one single tablespoon of oil. Pork belly 4 minutes without disturbing it, the edges brown and curl.
If there is more than 2 tablespoons of fat, pour off the excess. Keep the meat in the wok.
Raise to maximum heat. Chillies and garlic, 15 seconds.
All the cabbage at once, 2 minutes, turning constantly. The edges should brown in places.
Light soy sauce, dark soy sauce, sugar, a pinch of salt. Another 1 minute.
Vinegar poured onto the hot side of the wok, never into the middle. Toss 20 seconds and serve.
no: The pork fat replaces the oil.
Hence the single tablespoon at the start. Medium heat for the pork, maximum heat the moment the cabbage goes in. Never a lid, and salt only at step 7.
Vinegar on the side of the wok.
In the middle it dilutes; on the hot side it vaporises and perfumes everything. That is the move that separates a decent cabbage from the one you get in small restaurants.
For Chloé
Whole chillies rather than halved, lifted out before serving. They perfume the oil without releasing their heat.

g: Soft or silken tofu, in 3 cm cubes

g.t: Definitely not firm. Good mapo has tofu that wobbles.
The soul of the dish. Look for 郫縣 on the label, not a generic chilli sauce.
Wrinkled dry black beans, not the canned ones sitting in their liquid.
Not 250. The tofu already releases plenty of water.

g: Cornstarch slaked in 4 tbsp cold water
Garlic shoots or spring onion, in lengths
s: Toast the Sichuan peppercorns in a dry pan for 2 minutes, crush them in a mortar. Set aside in a bowl, they do not go into the pan.
Salted water at a simmer, not a boil. Slide in the tofu, 3 minutes. Drain and leave to drain a good 5 minutes in the colander.
Start the rice.
Oil in the wok over high heat. Brown the beef 5 minutes, crushing it, until it is brown and dry.
Lower to medium heat. Doubanjiang, 1 minute 30, the oil should turn deep red. Then douchi, garlic and ginger, 30 seconds.
Deglaze with the Shaoxing, pour in the stock and the soy sauce. Bring to a simmer.
Slide in the tofu. From here on do not stir with a spatula, push the wok back and forth.
Simmer 4 to 5 minutes. Watch the level: if it has risen, let it reduce 2 to 3 minutes uncovered.|Never thicken before the tofu has finished releasing its water
Pour in a third of the cornstarch, wait for a proper rolling boil, repeat twice.
Garlic shoots, one last push of the wok, serve. Everyone grinds their own Sichuan pepper and adds chilli oil at the table.
no: Cornstarch in three goes, at a full boil.
It only sets at a rolling boil. At a simmer it stays in suspension and the sauce turns liquid again as it cools. Whisk the bowl each time, it settles to the bottom within a minute.
For Chloé

The doubanjiang is already down to 1½ tablespoons and the Sichuan pepper stays out of the cooking. You make up for it in your own bowl with the chilli oil. That is how it is served in many Chengdu restaurants.
Adults-only version
Go up to 3 tablespoons of doubanjiang and add 1 teaspoon of chilli flakes with the garlic.

g: Ya cai, rinsed and squeezed dry

g.t: A small soft packet, usually in the dry goods aisle. It is what makes the difference.
Not tahini. Darker, from toasted seeds, and it separates in the jar.

s: Toast the Sichuan peppercorns in a dry pan for 2 minutes, crush them in a mortar.
Wok over high heat. Minced pork crushed with the spatula, 8 to 10 minutes. It must lose all its water, brown and turn almost crisp.
Add the ya cai, the Shaoxing and the dark soy sauce. Toss 3 minutes. Keep warm.
Build the sauce directly in the three serving bowls. Whisk with a fork to loosen the sesame paste with the hot stock.
Blanch the choy sum 2 minutes, lift it out. Cook the noodles in the same water.
Drain the noodles without rinsing and lay them on the sauce. Add pork, choy sum, spring onion, peanuts.
Serve in layers and mix at the table.
no: The sauce waits at the bottom of the bowl.
It never cooks and it is never tossed with the noodles in a pan. The diner does the mixing. If building three bowls feels fussy, mix everything in a large bowl and divide it, the result is identical.
The meat really has to dry out.
Those 8 to 10 minutes are the step everyone cuts short, and the one that counts.
For Chloé
Build her bowl with no chilli oil and only a pinch of Sichuan pepper. Make up for it with half a tablespoon of sesame paste and a splash of stock.

g.t: One lengthways cut per piece, strips of 4 to 5 cm. Keep the fat.

s: Cut the pork into 4 to 5 cm strips, lengthways. Score diagonally every 2 cm without cutting all the way through.
Marinade: hoisin, soy sauce, 2 tbsp of the honey, Shaoxing, grated garlic, five-spice.
Coat the pork, cover, 4 hours in the fridge, ideally overnight.
Oven at 200°C, 30 minutes, turning and basting every 10 minutes. Without an oven: covered pan, 25 minutes over medium heat, turning often.
Brush with the remaining honey, let it caramelise 5 minutes.
Blanch the bok choy 3 minutes, then stir-fry 2 minutes with garlic and a drizzle of oil.
Rest the meat 5 minutes before slicing it thinly.
no: The diagonal scoring.
The marinade penetrates far better and the honey catches in the cuts.
If the marinade burns before the end.
Lower the heat and cover. Char siu should be lacquered, not charred.

g.t: The central rib stays tough whatever you do; strip the leaves by pulling along the stem.

s: Strip the leaves from the central rib, tear them into large pieces.
Wok over very high heat with the neutral oil. Garlic 20 seconds, no more.
All the kale at once. Salt and toss for 1 minute.
Pour the Shaoxing onto the hot sides, cover immediately, 1 minute.
Uncover, oyster sauce and sugar, 1 minute. The leaves should be bright green and firm.
Off the heat, a drizzle of sesame oil.
no: Fermented bean curd variation.
Crush one cube of red fermented bean curd with a teaspoon of its liquid, in place of the oyster sauce. That is the classic Hong Kong treatment for leafy greens.
For Chloé
Kale is distinctly bitter. Blanching the leaves for 1 minute before stir-frying removes a good part of the bitterness, at the cost of a little crunch.

g.t: You bone them yourself: the bones go into the stock and the stock makes the sauce. Keep the skin aside.
Potato starch 馬鈴薯澱粉 gives an even crisper shell, both are in the same aisle.
Not orthodox for a Vietnamese dish, but it is what the original recipe does and it works.

g: The bones from the 3 thighs, chopped
Spring onion, whites and greens separated
s: Bone the thighs and remove the skin. Chop the bones with a heavy knife.|Chopped bones release their marrow and gelatine; left whole they will give nothing but warm water in twenty minutes

Bones, garlic clove and 400 ml water in a pan. Bring to the boil and let it boil uncovered while you prepare everything else.|This express stock is the only real advance work in the recipe, so start it first
Cut each thigh into four pieces.

Dry the pieces on kitchen paper, salt them, then roll them in the cornstarch at the last moment. Tap off the excess.|Floured in advance, the chicken sweats and the cornstarch turns into a sticky paste that will never crisp

Oil and butter in a large pan over medium-high heat. Lay the pieces in a single layer and do not touch them for 2 minutes.|The starch shell takes two minutes to set; stir before that and it comes away and stays on the bottom of the pan

Colour them on all sides, 6 to 8 minutes in total. They should be golden and already crisp.|And they are, without the skin, which is the whole point of the starch: chicken skin takes much longer to dry out and render its fat

Add the chopped garlic then the spring onion whites. Let them release their water and wait for the pan to go dry again.|If you add the sugar while there is still water, it dissolves instead of caramelising and you get a pale syrup

Add the sugar and the 2 tbsp of water. Let it melt and take colour without stirring, to a deep amber.|If it catches a little on the bottom that is fine, deglazing will lift it all. A caramel that turns dark brown, on the other hand, is bitter and beyond rescue

Lower the heat, then deglaze with the rice vinegar and the soy sauce, scraping the bottom with a spatula.|Poured onto a caramel at full heat, liquid spits violently: move your face back and lower the heat first

Add a ladle of strained stock, then a second if needed. The cornstarch that came off the chicken thickens the sauce by itself.|No extra thickening is useful, and the sauce thickens fast: go one ladle at a time
Let it reduce 2 to 3 minutes until the sauce coats the pieces and gleams.
Off the heat, pepper generously, squeeze in the half lemon and scatter the spring onion greens.|Acidity at the end is what stops the dish being merely sweet and salty
no: Where this recipe comes from.
It is Eloy Spinnler's caramel chicken, his "lazy dish", adapted from 4 to 3 servings. Caramel chicken is Vietnamese in origin, and the knob of butter in the pan is a liberty the author takes himself.
The starch replaces the skin.

The central idea of the dish. You remove the skin, which would need a long drying time to crisp, and replace it with a cornstarch shell that crisps in two minutes. Bonus: what comes off it thickens the sauce at the end, with nothing added.
No onion.

The original recipe has a shallot alongside the garlic and spring onion whites. I took it out and raised the garlic to two cloves. The dish loses nothing, the caramel and the soy sauce already carry plenty.
A bone stock in twenty minutes.
It looks superfluous and it is the difference between a caramel-soy sauce and a real sauce. You have the bones to hand, the water boils while you cut everything up, it costs nothing.
For Chloé

No chilli, a sweet-salty dish children eat very happily. Boned and cut into four, the pieces are already her size. Go easy on the pepper in her portion, and serve the lemon on the side rather than over the top.
pouletcaramel.p: Plain rice, and if you want to do it properly, crispy rice: spread day-old cooked rice in a thin layer in an oiled pan and leave it untouched for 6 to 8 minutes.

g.t: At the wet market, for a few dollars. Ask for a mix of marrow bones and shin bones: the marrow gives fat and flavour, the shin gives gelatine.
The sinewy offcuts butchers sell very cheaply. They are what give the stock body.

g: Whole leek, split and well washed

g.t: It is not there to make the stock tomatoey but to replace the colour and sweet base that onions would bring. See the notes.

s: Preheat the oven to 220°C. Spread the bones and trimmings on a tray, in a single layer, with a drizzle of oil.|Piled up they steam and stay pale. Every piece needs to touch the metal

Roast 45 to 50 minutes, turning halfway. They should be deep brown, close to mahogany.|This is where the colour of the final stock is decided, and nowhere else. Pale bones will give grey water however long you cook them afterwards
Add the vegetables and the tomato paste to the tray for the last 15 minutes only.|Added at the start they blacken and the stock turns bitter. A quarter of an hour is enough to colour them
Transfer the bones, trimmings and vegetables to a pot of at least 8 litres.

Set the empty tray over the heat, pour in 250 ml of water and scrape up every stuck-on bit with a spatula. Pour that into the pot.|Those browned bits are an enormous share of the flavour. A tray sent to the sink without being deglazed means a bland stock
Cover with the 3 litres of cold water, add the thyme, bay, parsley stalks and peppercorns.|Starting from cold: the impurities rise instead of setting into the meat
Bring up slowly, uncovered, and skim the grey foam relentlessly for the first 30 minutes.

Adjust the heat to the barest tremble, one bubble breaking now and then, around 85 to 90°C.|The point that decides everything. At the slightest boil the fat emulsifies into the liquid: the stock turns cloudy and greasy, and it will never be clear again
Leave 6 hours without stirring. Top up with hot water if the bones become exposed.
Strain through a fine sieve lined with a cloth, never pressing the solids.|Pressing forces fine particles through the cloth and clouds the stock permanently. You let it drip
Cool quickly, then a night in the fridge. The fat sets into a disc and lifts off in one piece.
Do not salt it.|The author's advice, and it is right: the stock will reduce in whatever you use it for, and salt added now would become impossible to control
For a more concentrated fond, reduce by half or by two thirds, uncovered, after straining.
no: Never a boil, for six hours.

That is the only real rule. A cloudy stock is not a badly seasoned stock, it is a stock that boiled: the agitation breaks the fat into droplets that stay in suspension. If your hob will not go low enough, move the pot half off the burner.
No onion, and what replaces it.

The original recipe calls for three onions, three shallots and a leek. I kept the leek, which has neither the taste nor the texture of onion, and removed the rest. What was missing is the brown colour and sweet base that roasted onion brings: the two tablespoons of tomato paste caramelised on the tray supply both, and it is a classic brown-stock move anyway.
Where to find bones in Hong Kong.

At the wet market, for almost nothing. Ask for sawn 牛骨, specifying a mix of marrow and shin bones, plus 牛筋 for the trimmings. Hong Kong butchers sell them routinely, bone soups being part of the local cooking.
Stock or fond?

Both words mean the same thing here. Roasting the bones before wetting them technically makes it a brown fond; without roasting you get a white stock, milder, which suits poultry and pale sauces. For a bourguignon, a navarin or an osso buco, the roasted version is the one you want.
Keeping it.

Five days in the fridge under its layer of fat, which protects it. Three months in the freezer: freeze part of it in ice cube trays so you have 30 ml doses to hand, and the rest in 250 ml portions. Reduced to a glace, it keeps far longer still.
For Chloé
A ladle of hot stock with vermicelli and a little soft carrot, and you have her dinner on the evenings she does not want anything.
fondboeuf.p: It is a base, not a dish. It transforms the beef bourguignon, the navarin, the osso buco and every brown sauce in the book. Wherever a recipe says "beef stock", this is what it wants.

g.t: Whole, not peeled. The heads and shells make the entire sauce.

s: Peel the prawns. Keep the heads and shells, chill the meat.
Oil in a sauté pan over high heat. Heads and shells 5 minutes, crushing them with the spatula to squeeze the juices out of the heads. They turn a deep orange-red.
Pour in the cognac and flambé, or let it evaporate for 1 minute.
Carrot, fennel and garlic, 5 minutes. Then the tomato paste, 2 minutes, it should darken slightly.
White wine, reduce by half. Add the chopped tomatoes, water, tarragon, cayenne. Season.
Simmer 25 minutes covered.
Pass through a fine sieve, pressing hard with a ladle. Discard the shells. Reduce uncovered for 10 minutes until the sauce coats.
Butter and oil in a very hot pan. Sear the prawns 1 minute 30 per side.
Pour the hot sauce over the prawns, toss 30 seconds off the heat, serve.
no: The prawns finish in the sauce, they do not cook in it.
Thirty seconds too long and they turn rubbery. The sauce must be completely finished before you touch the pan.
No onion or shallot.
The aromatic base is built on carrot, fennel and garlic. The fennel supplies the sweetness the onion used to give, so do not skip it.
Tarragon in Hong Kong.
Hard to find fresh at the wet market. Dried does the job perfectly well, and city'super and Oliver's carry it fresh.

g: Chuck or shoulder, in 5 cm cubes

g.t: French lardons are rare in HK. Buy thick-sliced smoked belly and cut them yourself.

s: Take the meat out an hour ahead. Dry each cube on kitchen paper, genuinely dry, then salt it.
Render the lardons in a dry casserole, 5 minutes. Lift them out, keep the fat.
Oil and high heat. Brown the meat in three batches, never more than six or seven cubes at a time, 2 minutes per side to a deep brown. Set aside.
Medium heat. Carrots, celery and garlic, 6 minutes in the browned juices.
Return the meat and lardons. Dust over the flour, 2 minutes. Tomato paste, 1 minute.
Pour in the wine, scrape the bottom with a wooden spoon. Boil 3 minutes.
Stock, thyme, bay. The liquid should come level with the meat without drowning it.
Cover, simmer 2 h 30 over very low heat. The surface should barely tremble.|If it boils, the meat turns stringy
Twenty minutes before the end, fry the halved mushrooms in the butter over high heat, 6 minutes. Salt at the end. Add them to the casserole.
If the sauce is too thin, uncover and reduce 15 minutes. Parsley as you serve.
no: Dry the meat and brown it in three batches.
Wet meat does not colour, it boils. All the flavour is decided in those first ten minutes.
The mushrooms are cooked separately.
Thrown in raw they release their water, go grey and wash out the sauce.
No onion.
The base is built on carrot, celery and garlic, and the garnish makes up for it with more mushrooms, 400 g instead of 250.
The wine.
You do not need a burgundy in Hong Kong. A dry, full-bodied red is enough. Avoid sweet or heavily oaked wines.
Better the next day.
Do not hesitate to make it the day before.

g.t: One per person. Whole, thick breasts, definitely not thin fillets: they cook gently and stay juicy, which a thin fillet will not forgive. Boneless thighs also work, with 10 minutes more simmering.
Kept whole, trimming only the hard end of the stem. Whole they stay meaty; sliced they release their water and vanish.
It replaces the shallots of the original recipe. See the notes.
The addition that changes everything: it thickens the sauce and gives it depth. Off the heat, or it will string.

s: Do not wash the mushrooms under water. Wipe them one by one with kitchen paper and trim the hard end of the stem.|A mushroom is a sponge: run it under water and it fills up, then releases it all in the pan instead of colouring
Preheat a heavy pan over medium heat for 3 minutes, then add the sunflower oil.|A properly hot pan brings the oil to temperature in seconds, so it is not sitting and heating for too long

Colour the breasts 3 minutes without touching them. Turn them, add a single pinch of salt, and colour 3 minutes on the other side.|Salt only at that moment: salted raw, they release their water and stop browning

Lift them out. They are not cooked through and should not be, they will finish in the sauce.|That is the whole point of the method: the cooking through happens covered, over low heat, not in a hot pan
Turn the heat to low and keep it there until the end of the recipe.|The point the video insists on, and it is right: everything from here on happens over low heat, so as not to dehydrate the chicken
Put the leek and the butter in the pan, with the paprika and the pepper. Stir so the spices spread through the butter, then sweat for 2 minutes.
Add the crushed garlic, stir and cook 1 minute.
Add the whole mushrooms and stir. They will absorb all the butter within seconds.|That is normal and expected: they give it back as they release their water
Keep stirring until the bottom of the pan starts to go dry. That is the signal to deglaze.
Deglaze with the cider vinegar. Scrape the bottom with a spatula to lift every browned bit.|Those browned bits are what will give the sauce its body; left stuck on, they do nothing
Wait until the vinegar has completely evaporated before adding the stock.|Adding liquid too early traps the vinegar's acidity in the sauce, which will stay sharp
Pour in the stock and stir. Thanks to the lifted browned bits it thickens slightly on its own.
Return the chicken breasts and lay 2 or 3 sprigs of thyme on top.
Cover with the tightest-fitting lid you have and simmer 20 minutes over low heat.|A badly fitting lid lets the steam escape, the liquid reduces too fast and the chicken dries out
Take off the lid, lift out the breasts and remove the thyme sprigs.
Add the cream and the mustard, stir to a smooth sauce, still over low heat.|Mustard must never boil: it turns bitter and splits. If the sauce starts to bubble, pull the pan off the heat
Let it simmer gently while you chop the parsley.|Fresh herbs are chopped at the last minute, otherwise they lose most of their aroma before they reach the dish
Throw the parsley into the sauce, then the grated cheese off the heat, stirring until it has melted.
Return the breasts to the sauce to warm through, and serve.
no: Low heat from start to finish, apart from the browning.

Three minutes over medium heat to sear each side, and never again after that. Chicken breast is lean: past 70°C at the core it contracts and squeezes out its moisture, and no sauce rescues dehydrated meat. The twenty covered minutes over low heat are what keep it juicy.
Whole breasts, not thin fillets.
A thin fillet is cooked through before it has browned. A thick whole breast takes the browning and then the slow cooking, and that is the only way to get both a golden crust and a tender centre.
No shallot.

The original recipe builds its base on two shallots. Finely sliced leek white replaces them: the same melting sweetness, the same way of carrying the butter and paprika, and nothing of the onion about it. The garlic goes up to three cloves.
Never wash mushrooms.

They absorb water like a sponge and then release it into the pan, where they boil instead of browning. Kitchen paper and thirty seconds is all it takes. And keep them whole: they shrink a great deal as it is.
The grated cheese at the end.
Forty grams of gruyère or parmesan off the heat, and the sauce goes from a decent cream to something that coats and has depth. In the heat, it would string.
For Chloé

Nothing spicy, the paprika is sweet and the mustard disappears entirely into the cream. Cut her breast into thick slices and spoon plenty of sauce over. The whole mushrooms can be halved on her plate.
pouletcreme.p: Rice, fresh pasta or steamed potatoes. The sauce is generous and that is the point: you need something to mop it up with.

panga.n: Panga fillet with a herb crust

g.t: In chilled trays at AEON under this name, or frozen elsewhere as cream dory 多利魚. Chilled trays are almost always thawed: treat them as frozen.
It is not a seasoning, it is the glue for the crust. In a thin layer you will not taste it.

s: If the fillets are frozen, thaw them in the fridge on a rack overnight, never in water or the microwave. If they are fresh, go straight to the next step.|Fast thawing bursts the fibres: the fillet releases even more water and the flesh turns woolly

If a brown-red strip runs along the flank, cut it away on a slant, 2 or 3 mm deep. Supermarket trays are already trimmed, whole wet-market fillets never are.|That strip is what carries the muddy taste people hold against panga

Set the fillets on a double layer of kitchen paper, salt both sides, cover with another double layer and rest a light board on top. 20 minutes in the fridge for frozen, 10 minutes is enough for fresh.|The step that decides everything with frozen fish, which is waterlogged, often with water added at freezing. Without pressing it comes back out during cooking, soaks the crust from below and the fish boils in its own juices. On a fresh fillet the salt mainly firms the flesh
Change the paper and dry one last time. The surface should be matt, not shiny.

Look at the thickness of the fillet: it is always thick at one end and very thin at the other. Fold the thin part under the fillet to get a roughly even thickness.|Without that fold, the tail is dry and woolly by the time the back is just cooked. It is the shape of the fish, not a cooking fault
Preheat the oven to 210°C, fan. Set a rack on a tray, or failing that use baking paper.|Flat on the metal, the underside of the fillet sits in the little water that still comes out
Finely chop the parsley, chives and garlic, mix them with the panko, parmesan and lemon zest.
Pour in the melted butter and mix with your fingertips to the texture of damp sand.|Too much butter and the crumb clumps into a paste that will not crisp; too little and it burns as dry powder
Brush the tops of the fillets with a thin layer of mustard.|It is what holds the crust on. Without mustard the crust slides straight off the fillet as you serve it
Press the crust onto the top only, firmly, 5 mm thick. Nothing on the sides or underneath.
Bake 12 to 14 minutes depending on thickness, 14 to 16 for a fresh fillet, which is often thicker and less watery.

It is done when the flesh separates into large flakes under a fork tip but stays slightly pearly at the core.|Panga goes from cooked to cotton wool in two minutes. Take it out when the centre still looks barely translucent, it will finish outside the oven
If the crust is not golden enough while the fish is cooked, 60 to 90 seconds under the grill without taking your eyes off it.
Rest 2 minutes. Serve the lemon in wedges on the side.|Lemon juice poured over the crust softens it within seconds. Everyone squeezes their own
New potatoes: halved, olive oil, salt, 30 minutes at 210°C. They go into the oven before the fish.
no: The "fresh" in Hong Kong supermarkets.

The chilled trays at AEON or Wellcome, labelled 越南鯰魚柳, are thawed fish, not fresh fish: the use-by date two days after the packing date says so. Milky liquid in the bottom of the tray confirms it. Treat them as frozen, twenty minutes of pressing, even though they are sold in the chilled aisle. The genuinely fresh option is a whole fillet from the wet market.
Fresh or frozen, it is not the same fish.

Frozen, panga is waterlogged, often with water added at packing: twenty minutes of pressing under a weight, no argument, otherwise the crust soaks from below. Fresh, it releases far less: ten minutes of salt is enough, and it mainly firms the flesh. On the other hand a fresh fillet arrives whole, with its brown strip along the flank, which has to come off. Supermarket frozen fillets are already trimmed.
The brown strip, on a fresh fillet.

It is the red muscle and the fat running along the flank. They concentrate the muddy taste people hold against panga, and they come off in twenty seconds with a knife. It is the difference between a neutral fish and one with an aftertaste.
The mustard is glue.
A thin layer on top, and the crust holds all the way to the plate. Same principle as the double breading on the cordon bleu: the crumb needs something to grip.
If you want to trade up.
The method is exactly the same with cod, hake or pollock, which have more flavour and firmer flesh. Simply allow 2 minutes less cooking and a shorter press, those fish are far less watery.
For Chloé
No bones, a very mild flavour, and the golden parmesan crust is what wins her over. Let her press the crumb onto the fillets, it is messy and easy. Her lemon on the side.
panga.p: The roast new potatoes, which cook in the same oven, and a green salad. A drizzle of raw olive oil over the fish as you serve does no harm.

g.t: Thick and even. A thin, tapered breast will not butterfly.
In the Japanese aisle of any Hong Kong supermarket, and cheaper than imported breadcrumbs. Lighter, crisper, and it drinks less oil.

s: Lay a breast flat, palm flat on top, and cut it horizontally with a thin knife without going through the far edge. Open it like a book.

Slide the opened escalope into a freezer bag and flatten it to 5 mm with a rolling pin or the base of a pan, working from the centre outwards.|Below 5 mm the meat tears and the cheese will escape through the hole; above it, the centre is raw by the time the crust is golden
Season the inside with salt and pepper, spread a thin layer of mustard.

Lay on a slice of ham, the cheese on top, then a second slice of ham, leaving 2 cm of bare chicken all the way round.|The ham wraps the cheese, and that is what holds the leak back. Cheese touching the edge will always find a way out
Fold over and seal the edges by pressing firmly with your fingertips all the way round.
Three shallow bowls: flour, beaten eggs, panko. Through the flour, tapping off the excess, then the egg, then the panko, pressing it on well.
Go through the egg and the panko a second time, paying particular attention to the edge.|The double breading is the anti-leak insurance; it is always the side that gives way

Chill 30 minutes, uncovered, on a rack or a plate.|The step everyone skips and the one that decides everything: the breading dries, hardens and bonds to the meat. Without that rest it comes away in the pan and the cheese goes with it
Preheat the oven to 180°C. Oil and butter in a large pan over medium heat.|Too hot and the breading is black in three minutes while the centre is still cold
Check the temperature by dropping in a crumb of panko: it should turn golden in 3 or 4 seconds, sizzling gently, not crackling violently.
4 to 5 minutes per side, to an even golden brown. Turn once only.|Turning repeatedly lifts the still-fragile breading
Transfer to a rack set over a tray and finish in the oven for 8 minutes.|The rack stops the underside going soft in its own steam, and the oven cooks the centre without pushing the colour further
Rest 3 minutes before cutting, or the melted cheese squirts out. Serve with the lemon and the salad.
no: Why the cheese escapes.

There is never one reason, there are four, and they add up: an escalope flattened too thin and pierced, cheese touching the edge, single instead of double breading, and above all no chilling. Do all four properly and nothing comes out.
Panko, not breadcrumbs.

It is the best accident of cooking in Hong Kong: panko is everywhere, for almost nothing, while French breadcrumbs are an imported product. And it gives a frankly better crust, airier and less greasy.
Prepare them ahead.

Breaded and wrapped they keep 24 hours in the fridge, which actually improves how the breading holds. Raw and breaded they freeze very well separated by baking paper, and cook from frozen with 5 extra minutes in the oven.
For Chloé

One of the few dishes a six-year-old can make almost entirely. Give her the three breading bowls, she dips and turns, it is messy and that is exactly the point. Make hers smaller, with half a breast, and it will cook in 3 minutes a side.
cordonbleu.p: Green salad and a lemon wedge are enough. If you want something more substantial, sautéed potatoes or mash, but not both, the cordon bleu is rich already.

g.t: 無鹽牛油. Out of the fridge an hour ahead, it should give under a finger without being melted.
The extra yolk is what gives the soft centre.
Weigh it, never measure by volume. Hong Kong is humid, flour packs down and a measuring cup can have you adding a third too much.

g: Dark chocolate 60 to 70%, chopped with a knife

g.t: A chopped bar, not chips. The irregular pieces make molten pools and the fine dust marbles the dough.

s: Beat the soft butter with both sugars for 3 minutes, until the mixture pales and turns fluffy.
Add the whole egg, then the yolk, then the vanilla, mixing after each addition.
Mix the flour, baking soda and salt separately, then tip them onto the butter all at once.
Mix only until the flour disappears, not a second longer.|Overworked dough gives hard cookies
Fold in the chopped chocolate with a spatula.
Cover and rest in the fridge for 24 hours, 48 if you can. An hour is already better than nothing.
Preheat the oven to 180°C. Line the tray with baking paper.|Straight on the metal, the undersides brown long before the rest is cooked
Shape balls of about 55 g, the size of a golf ball, six per tray at most and well spaced.

Flatten each ball with your palm into a puck 2.5 cm thick, then leave the tray 15 minutes at room temperature while the oven heats.|A tall, chilled ball straight out of 24 h in the fridge has no time to spread: it bakes into a dome
Bake in the upper half of the oven, 10 to 12 minutes.

At 7 minutes, look. The pucks should have slumped and widened, the edges starting to set. If they are still domed, take the tray out and drop it flat onto the worktop from about twenty centimetres: the domes collapse at once. Return to the oven.|That is the rescue, and it works every time
Take them out when the edges are set and golden and the centre is still pale and visibly undercooked.|Take them out when they look raw in the middle
Scatter with flaky salt and leave 10 minutes on the hot tray without touching them. That is when they finish cooking and the centre sets.
no: The fridge rest changes everything.

Over 24 hours the flour hydrates completely and the sugars dissolve. The flavour moves from flat-sweet to caramel and toffee, and the cookie spreads less in the oven. The same dough baked immediately and baked the next day gives two different biscuits.
Take them out undercooked.
That is mistake number one. The hot tray goes on cooking them for a good five minutes. A cookie already golden in the centre in the oven will be dry once cold.
If they do not spread.

The downside of the 24-hour rest: the dough comes out of the fridge hard and cold, and a tall ball takes longer to melt than the oven takes to seize it. It then bakes into a pale dome with the underside browning on its own. Hence the 2.5 cm puck and the 15 minutes at room temperature before baking. And if it happens anyway, dropping the tray on the worktop at 7 minutes flattens them.
Small countertop oven.

In Hong Kong's small ovens the bottom element is very close to the tray. Baking paper is compulsory, rack in the upper half, and if the undersides darken too fast, a second cold tray slid underneath acts as a shield.
Chips or a bar.
Chips contain stabilisers that stop them melting, so they stay as hard dots. A bar chopped with a knife gives molten pools of chocolate and dust that colours the dough.
For Chloé
She can roll the balls, press a few chunks of chocolate on top before baking, and scatter the flaky salt as they come out. Rested dough rolls very well by hand and does not stick.
cookies.p: The raw dough keeps 3 days in the fridge and 3 months in the freezer as pre-rolled balls. Bake them straight from frozen, 2 minutes longer.

g.t: The high-gluten flour, in bags in every supermarket. It is what gives the doughnut its stringy crumb.
Between 35 and 38°C, warm to the finger. Above 50°C it kills the yeast.
Groundnut or sunflower. You need 6 cm of depth in a tall pan, not a frying pan.
For the white glaze.
For the glaze, added a spoonful at a time.
For the cinnamon-sugar version.

s: Dissolve the yeast and 1 tsp of the sugar in the warm milk. Leave 10 minutes: a foam should form on the surface.|If nothing foams, the yeast is dead and nothing will rescue the dough. Start again with a fresh sachet rather than carrying on
Mix the flour, remaining sugar and salt in a large bowl.
Pour in the yeasted milk, the eggs and the vanilla. Knead 5 minutes.

Add the soft butter piece by piece and knead another 8 to 10 minutes, until the dough is smooth and pulls away from the sides while still being tacky to the finger.|Do not add flour to make it less sticky: an enriched dough has to stay supple and slightly tacky, and that is exactly what makes it tender. More flour gives a dry, tight doughnut

Shape into a ball in an oiled bowl, cover, and leave to rise until doubled in volume.|In Hong Kong in November allow 1 h to 1 h 15, but keep watching: in a flat at 28°C it will be done in 45 minutes. Trust the volume, never the clock
Knock back with the flat of your hand and roll the dough out to 1.5 cm thick.|Thinner, it will not puff enough and the doughnut will be dry
Cut 8 cm discs, then punch out the centre with a 3 cm cutter. Keep the holes, they fry too.
Set each doughnut on its own square of baking paper.|That is what lets you slide it into the oil without deforming it: a risen doughnut lifted by hand collapses and never recovers its shape
Cover and leave to rise 30 to 45 minutes.

Test with a floured fingertip: the dent should come back slowly and incompletely. If it springs back at once, wait longer. If it does not come back at all, it is too late and the doughnut will collapse in the oil.

Heat the oil to 175°C, 6 cm deep. Without a thermometer, a cube of bread should turn golden in 45 to 50 seconds.|The point that decides everything: below 165°C the doughnut drinks the oil and comes out greasy, above 190°C it is brown outside and raw inside

Lower in 3 doughnuts at a time, paper and all. The paper peels away by itself after a few seconds, lift it out with tongs.|More than three at once drops the oil temperature by twenty degrees, and everything else follows
75 to 90 seconds per side, turning once only.
Look for the pale ring around the equator: that is the signature of a well-risen, well-fried doughnut.|No white ring means either over-risen dough or oil that was too hot
Drain on a rack, never on kitchen paper.|Flat on paper, the underside cooks in its own steam and goes soft within two minutes

Cinnamon sugar: roll the doughnuts in the mixture while still hot. Glaze: mix the icing sugar and milk a spoonful at a time to the texture of thick cream, and dip the doughnuts while warm.|Glazed piping hot, the glaze melts and runs straight off; glazed cold, it will not stick
no: Oil temperature is the whole subject.

A greasy doughnut is not a badly cooked doughnut, it is one fried too cold: it stays in the oil too long and absorbs it. A cooking thermometer at 60 HKD solves the problem for good. And the oil drops with every batch, so let it come back up in between.
The white ring.
Look at any photograph of a bakery doughnut: there is always a pale band all the way round, where the dough floated clear of the oil. That is your visual quality check, and it does not lie.
Hong Kong's humidity works in your favour.
The rising times in European recipes are consistently too long here. In summer the dough can double in 35 minutes. Judge by volume and by the fingertip dent, not by the timer.
Eat them the same day.
A raised doughnut peaks an hour after frying and is already disappointing the next day. That is the nature of the thing, no airtight box changes it. Make half a batch rather than keeping any.
For Chloé

The cutter is hers. She can also roll the hot doughnuts in the cinnamon sugar. Keep her away from the pan of oil, though, and fry the holes first: they are done in 40 seconds a side and they are her reward while the rest cooks.
donuts.p: The dough scraps re-form into a ball, rest 20 minutes and fry again. Only rework them once: beyond that the dough turns elastic and the doughnuts rubbery.
